extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, in-house counsel and patentees considering UPC litigation or opt-out strategy
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and procedural guidance on litigating European and Unitary patents before the Unified Patent Court (UPC), including jurisdiction, procedure, remedies, appeals, and the practicalities and strategic considerations for opting out validated European patents from UPC jurisdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single-court jurisdiction and cross-border enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: The UPC operates as a single court with jurisdiction over multiple European countries; an infringement action brought at the UPC could cover all UPC participating countries and may lead to a single injunction across all participating countries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advantage for patentees is reduced cost compared with bringing separate national actions and avoidance of inconsistent national decisions. Note: Spain and Croatia are exceptions; non-participating countries remain under national courts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Litigation language and translation considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents granted in English are likely to be litigated in English, reducing translation costs and enabling English-speaking litigants to participate fully.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local/regional divisions hear cases in official languages of the host country or other languages designated by the division; all divisions have designated English. Parties may request the language of the patent, subject to court approval and consideration of defendant position. The central division hears cases in the language the patent was granted.

rubrics_metrics.name: UPC powers to obtain evidence and on-site inspection (saise-contrefaçon)
rubrics_metrics.description: The UPC can order alleged infringers to disclose relevant material under their control and can enable evidence gathering via a saise-contrefaçon procedure where court officials can gain access without notice to business premises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful for proving infringement; evidence orders may include disclosure of origin/distribution channels, quantities, prices and identities of third parties. Confidentiality protection measures may be available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promised case timescales / speed of procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: The Rules of Procedure envisage first instance decisions within 12 to 15 months and a similar amount of time for appeal. Initial first instance decisions have been issued in the promised timeframe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: UPC procedure is designed to be faster than many national courts; parties should plan for compressed deadlines in the Written Procedure and Interim Procedure phases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Costs recovery against losing party
rubrics_metrics.description: The UPC has the power to award costs against a losing party; if a patentee successfully establishes infringement they can recover a proportion of their legal costs from the losing party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Costs are expected to be reasonable and proportionate; recoverable levels are subject to further guidance and links provided by the court.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality of judicial panels and appellate structure
rubrics_metrics.description: First-instance UPC cases will be heard by a panel of three experienced and specialist IP judges (with at least one national IP specialist judge) and the Court of Appeal sits as a panel of five experienced appeal judges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expectation of high-quality, specialist decisions from the outset and a central Court of Appeal in Luxembourg.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unitary Patent exclusivity of UPC jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Unitary Patents can only be litigated in the Unified Patent Court; by selecting a Unitary Patent the proprietor is effectively choosing to use the UPC and there is no option to opt out of the UPC for a Unitary Patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selecting unitary protection is a conscious jurisdictional choice — strategize accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: UPC jurisdiction over validated European patents and opt-out availability
rubrics_metrics.description: The UPC has jurisdiction over European patents validated in UPC participating countries unless the European Patent has been proactively opted out; opting out is only available for national validations of a European Patent and is not an option for a Unitary Patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The ability to opt out will cease after a transitional period (initially 7 years), so timing of opt-out requests matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: National courts' exclusive jurisdiction for opted-out or non-participating countries
rubrics_metrics.description: National courts have exclusive jurisdiction over national validations of European patents which have been opted out of the UPC and for national validations in countries not participating in the UPC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Opting out a European patent preserves national enforcement only; consider cross-border enforcement needs when deciding to opt out.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court structure: central, local and regional divisions
rubrics_metrics.description: The UPC comprises a Court of First Instance (central division and local/regional divisions) and a Court of Appeal. Local divisions handle infringement in individual countries; regional divisions handle multiple countries; the central division has special responsibilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local divisions confirmed in multiple countries (list provided). Parties can agree where to bring actions subject to rules and exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Central division sections and allocation by classification
rubrics_metrics.description: The central division is split between France, Germany and Italy (Paris, Munich, Milan sections). Paris deals with electronics, software and physics; Munich with mechanical engineering; Milan with chemistry, pharmaceuticals, biotechnology and human necessities. Allocation is by the first-mentioned classification code.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a patent has classification codes in multiple fields it will be allocated to the section responsible for the first-mentioned classification code — consider classification when predicting central division allocation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may represent parties before the UPC
rubrics_metrics.description: Any lawyer authorised to practice before a court of a participating country and any suitably qualified European Patent Attorney may represent a party before any division and the Court of Appeal of the UPC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: European Patent Attorneys with UPC qualifications are eligible; firms with both national lawyers and European Patent Attorneys can represent clients across divisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division responsibilities and when central division hears infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: In general infringement actions are brought before a local or regional division. Exceptionally, infringement actions can be brought before the central division if (a) the parties agree or (b) the defendant does not have a place of business in any UPC participating country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If defendant counter-claims for invalidity, local/regional division may hear invalidity as part of same action, refer counterclaim to central division, or refer entire case. Parties should consider strategic forum selection, and the possibility of referral.

rubrics_metrics.name: Where claimants must bring infringement actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Claimants must bring infringement actions in the local/regional division where the actual or threatened infringement has occurred or may occur, or where the defendant has its residence or principal place of business; if defendant has no residence in a participating country the claimant may bring the action where the infringement occurred or before the central division if no local/regional division exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical implications for venue selection; if a counterclaim for revocation is filed it must be brought in the local/regional division hearing the infringement action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interaction between revocation, infringement and declaration of non-infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: To challenge validity other than as a counterclaim, an action must be brought at the central division. An action seeking a declaration of non-infringement must be brought at the central division, which will stay the action if an infringement action between the same parties is brought before a local/regional division within 3 months.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strategic timing matters: a central division non-infringement action can be stayed by subsequent local infringement proceedings — plan filings with this rule in mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language of proceedings in central and appellate courts
rubrics_metrics.description: The central division hears cases in the language the patent concerned was granted. The Court of Appeal generally uses the same language as the Court of First Instance, except in exceptional circumstances or by party agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties can agree to use the language in which the patent was granted, subject to court approval; the position of the defendant is particularly important when language is contested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicable law for validity and infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Articles 138 and 139 of the EPC represent the applicable law for validity. The law for infringement is the national law of a participating country determined by the nationality or place of business of the first named applicant at the time of filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: UPC is not bound by national precedent and will develop its own case law; Rome I Regulation applies to contractual matters (licences/co-ownership agreements) allowing parties to choose governing law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeals: scope, new evidence, and effect on decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Appeals to the Court of Appeal are available as of right on final decisions, decisions terminating proceedings as regards one party, and decisions on certain types of orders. Appeals are based on points of law and matters of fact, but new facts/evidence may only be introduced if they could not reasonably have been submitted in first instance. Appeals against final decisions suspend those decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Other orders may require leave to appeal or must be appealed with the final decision. The Court of Appeal may overturn or remit the case back to first instance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written/Interim/Oral Procedure and compressed deadlines
rubrics_metrics.description: UPC procedure comprises a Written Procedure (statements of case), an Interim Procedure (preparations for trial) and an Oral Procedure. The Rules include hard deadlines: 3 months to file a defence to an infringement action and a counterclaim for revocation; 2 months to file a reply to the defence and a defence to the counterclaim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties must be ready to act quickly in the Written Procedure to meet tight timetables; first-instance envisaged to complete in 12–15 months.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final remedies available from the UPC
rubrics_metrics.description: Final orders obtainable include revocation of a patent (entirely or partly), injunctions (including against intermediaries), recall, deprivation or destruction of infringing products and materials, and damages which are compensatory (lost profit, unfair profits and non-economic factors like moral prejudice may be considered).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Damages are compensatory not punitive; an infringer can avoid damages by demonstrating lack of knowledge or no reasonable grounds to know of infringement, though compensation or recovery of profits may still be ordered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interim orders and evidence preservation
rubrics_metrics.description: Interim orders available include interim injunctions to cease infringing activity, disclosure orders for documents/information, and evidence preservation orders (ex parte measures such as inspecting premises, taking samples, seizing products/materials/documents).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence preservation orders may be subject to a bond and applicants may have to compensate defendants if there was no infringement or if the applicant fails to pursue the case. Some interim orders may require national enforcement measures to be effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure of evidence standard
rubrics_metrics.description: If a party presents reasonable evidence sufficient to support its claims that necessary documents or information (relating to liability, quantum of damages or validity) are under the control of the opposing party or a third party, the court may order disclosure of the relevant material, with protective measures for confidential information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use disclosure orders when documentary evidence is in the control of the opponent or third parties; anticipate confidentiality protocols and protective measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof and reverse-burden in process patents
rubrics_metrics.description: As in civil litigation, any party seeking to rely on a fact has the burden of proving it and may rely on witnesses, experts, inspection, experiments or comparative tests, affidavits, documents, requests for information, and submissions. The burden of proof can be reversed if the subject-matter is a process for obtaining a new product and the infringing product is identical to the product produced by the patented process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider reverse-burden scenarios in process-patent enforcement where the accused product is identical to the product of a claimed process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of court-appointed experts
rubrics_metrics.description: The court may appoint court experts to provide expertise for specific aspects of the case; a list of approved experts is kept by the Registrar to guarantee independence and impartiality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court experts can be used to resolve technical disputes impartially; parties should anticipate and engage with the expert process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fees, cost-shifting and enforcement of orders
rubrics_metrics.description: The UPC is intended to be self-financing and court fees are payable (value-based fees). The UPC agreement states that reasonable and proportionate legal costs and other expenses incurred by the successful party shall as a general rule be borne by the unsuccessful party. Enforcement proceedings are governed by the law of the participating country where enforcement takes place, and the UPC can sanction non-compliance with recurring penalties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Calculate value-based fees and budget for possible cost orders; enforcement mechanisms and penalties vary by national law where enforcement occurs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arbitration and mediation options
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent mediation and arbitration centre is seated in Ljubljana and Lisbon, and a list of mediators and arbitrators is held by the UPC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider mediation/arbitration as alternatives or adjuncts to UPC litigation; lists of mediators/arbitrators are available via the UPC.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may bring an infringement action
rubrics_metrics.description: The patent proprietor is entitled to bring infringement actions. An exclusive licensee may bring an infringement action as long as the licence agreement does not prohibit it and it gives prior notice to the proprietor. A non-exclusive licensee may bring an infringement action if the licence agreement expressly permits it and it gives prior notice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check licence terms and give required prior notice before initiating UPC proceedings as a licensee.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opting out of UPC jurisdiction for validated European patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Patentees can file a request to opt out nationally validated European patents from the jurisdiction of the UPC. An opt out must be filed for each European patent to be opted out. If an opt out is not registered before the opening of the UPC, third parties may start actions at the UPC. After a UPC action has commenced, it is no longer possible to opt out. A filed opt out can be withdrawn so long as no national litigation has commenced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Opting out prevents UPC enforcement but preserves national court jurisdiction. Timing is critical: filing before UPC opening avoids third-party UPC suits; withdrawal is possible but limited by national actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic considerations for deciding to opt out
rubrics_metrics.description: Reasons to opt out: avoid a single central revocation action; avoid exposure to a new/unfamiliar court; concern about defending cost and adverse costs findings; concern about short UPC deadlines. Reasons not to opt out: desire to be involved in UPC development; avoid administrative burden and cost of opt out; to ensure central enforcement remains available and to prevent a third party commencing national action to prevent withdrawal of an opt out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance litigation risk, strategic involvement, administrative costs and enforcement needs when deciding whether to opt out. Consider industry-specific risk profiles and portfolio-wide implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical requirements and recommended safeguards for opt out requests
rubrics_metrics.description: Opt out requests are made in respect of all the 'states for which the European patent has been granted' and must list the name(s) and address(es) of the patent proprietor(s). If SPCs exist based on a patent, they and their owners must be named. A third party can challenge an opt out on the basis of wrong states/proprietor named or lack of consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendations to reduce risk of successful challenge: obtain clear consent from a duly authorised officer of each proprietor; provide original assignment documents where relevant; ensure up-to-date national registers reflecting the same proprietors as named in the opt out. For assignments after grant, carefully consider which documents establish whose consent is required for the opt out.
